definitions.definition: The Vedic offering-rite performed with fire, mantras and priests; in the Brāhmaṇas it is identified with the cosmic Person, with Prajāpati, with the year and with Viṣṇu ('puruṣo vai yajñaḥ', ŚB 1.3.2.1; 'yajño vai viṣṇuḥ').
Any of the prescribed offerings of the householder — the daily great sacrifices, the cooked-food, oblation and Soma sacrifices counted among the forty sacraments (GDh 8.14–21).

The hidden correspondence the Brāhmaṇas establish between an element of the rite, the cosmos and the person (e.g. the bricks of the altar = the days and nights of the year = the joints of Prajāpati); knowing the bandhu is what makes the rite effective.

The creator who, alone in the beginning, desired to multiply, heated himself with austerity and emitted the worlds and beings; exhausted and fallen apart after creating, he is the year and is rebuilt in the fire-altar and the sacrifice.
In Manu, the creator-lord who milked the syllables a-u-m and the Sāvitrī from the Vedas (MDh 2.76–77); one of the names by which the one supreme Person is called (MDh 12.123).

The twice-daily milk offering into the sacred fires by one who has set them up; the Brāhmaṇas explain it as healing the junction of day and night (ŚB 1.6.3.36), as an offering of 'truth in faith' when nothing else exists (ŚB 11.3.1.4), and as a cycle through the worlds and the body (ŚB 11.6.2).
Interiorized as the offering into the breaths at meals (ChU 5.19–24) and as the continuous 'inner Agnihotra' of speech and breath (KU 2.5).

The offering of the first morsels of a meal to the five breaths (prāṇa, vyāna, apāna, samāna, udāna) with svāhā, so that eating becomes an Agnihotra offered in all worlds and selves (ChU 5.19–24; Mahānārāyaṇa Up. = TA 10.69–70; Prāṇāgnihotra Up.).
The meal-rite of the twice-born incorporating the breath-oblations, prescribed in the Dharmasūtras' rules on eating.

The year-long building of the great brick fire-altar (often in the shape of a falcon) in five layers, explained in ŚB 6–10 as the rebuilding of Prajāpati who fell apart, so that the sacrificer builds and becomes an immortal self.
The consecration of the sacrificer before a Soma rite, by which the priests 'make him an embryo again' (AB 1.3); he keeps vows and is reborn at the final bath.
The consecration for sacrifice counted as the twice-born's third birth (MDh 2.169).
The gift to the officiating priests, the 'human gods', as oblations go to the gods (ŚB 2.2.2.6); it does not reach the world attained by knowledge (ŚB 10.5.4.16).
A sphere of existence or post-mortem state; the sacrificer constructs his future world through rites — 'a man is born into the world he has made' (ŚB 6.2.2.27).
Dying again in the other world; the Brāhmaṇas promise its conquest ('apa punarmṛtyuṃ jayati') to those who know or perform certain rites — the fire-altar, the Nāciketa fire (ŚB 10.4.3; TB 3.11.8).
Death personified; identified with the year, which wears away mortals' lives by days and nights (ŚB 10.4.3.1); his claims are limited by knowledge and rite.
The indirect, hidden name or form preferred by the gods — 'the gods love the cryptic and dislike the obvious' (ŚB 10.5.2.20; 14.6.11.2; AB 3.43).
One who sacrifices knowing that each rite builds a limb of his own (new) self, and who so sheds the mortal body like a snake its skin (ŚB 11.2.6.13).
One who sees the self in all beings and all beings in the self, and so attains self-rule (MDh 12.91).
The sovereignty over all beings attained by Brahman when it offered itself in all beings (ŚB 13.7.1.1).
The self-rule attained by the one who sacrifices to the self (MDh 12.91).
Meditation on a thing as something else ('let one meditate on the Real as Brahman'), by which one becomes what one meditates on (ŚB 10.6.3).
The knowledge of the correspondences (and of the self) by which one reaches the world beyond desire where fees and uninformed austerity do not reach (ŚB 10.5.4.16).
The lower knowledge (aparā vidyā) includes the four Vedas and six Vedāṅgas; the higher is that by which the imperishable is reached (MuU 1.1.4–5).
The purpose or resolve that constitutes a person: as his resolve at departure, so he becomes in the next world (ŚB 10.6.3.1).
The two 'great monsters/spirits' of Brahman by which it descended into the worlds; as far as name and form extend, so far extends the universe (ŚB 11.2.3).

cross_language.note: In Buddhism a link of dependent origination, a different doctrinal sense

definitions.definition: In the Brāhmaṇas: the sacred formulation and the Veda; also the first principle — 'in the beginning this was Brahman' (ŚB 11.2.3.1), 'Brahman the self-existent' (ŚB 10.6.5.9; 13.7.1.1; GB 1.1.1).
The supreme reached by self-knowledge and seeing the self in all (MDh 12.125); 'the one syllable is the supreme Brahman' (VDh 10.5).

In ritual contexts the body or trunk (of the altar, of the sacrificer) that the rite constructs; in the teachings of Śāṇḍilya and Aśvapati the inner self 'made of mind, with breath for body' (ŚB 10.6.3).
The self to be seen by yoga (YS 1.8), its own witness (MDh 8.84), one in all beings though appearing many like space in pots (YS 3.144).
The one self of the deity of which the many gods are limbs (Nirukta 7.4).
The highest dharma, attained by yoga (YS 1.8).
The highest of the means to the supreme good, foremost of all sciences, by which immortality is gained (MDh 12.85).
The supreme self whose subtlety the renouncer discerns by yoga (MDh 6.65).
The Person with whom the sacrifice is identical (ŚB 1.3.2.1); Puruṣa Nārāyaṇa who surpassed all beings by the human sacrifice (ŚB 13.6.1.1).
The supreme Person, ruler of all, subtler than the subtle, called by many names (MDh 12.122–123).

Breath as the vital power: the seers are the breaths (ŚB 6.1.1.1); the breath is the consecrated (KB 7.1); the one god is the breath, called 'that' (ŚB 11.6.3); the breaths are enumerated as five (prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, samāna).
The breath impelled by the body's fire that, striking the places of articulation, produces the phonemes (Pāṇinīya Śikṣā 6–9).
Speech as Prajāpati's own and second, sent forth to pervade all (PB 20.14.2); yoked with mind to carry the sacrifice (ŚB 1.4.4.7); speech as consecration (KB 7.1).
The object of grammar and phonetics; in the Mahābhāṣya the 'great god' who enters mortals, identity with whom is the aim of grammar.

Mind as the first existent — 'neither non-being nor being; there was only mind' (ŚB 10.5.3.1); the greater of the pair mind and speech (ŚB 1.4.4.7); the brahman priest's track of the sacrifice (ChU 4.16).
The eleventh sense, of the nature of both the organs of knowledge and of action (MDh 2.92), and the instigator of all action (MDh 12.4).
The creative heat by which Prajāpati and the primal waters brought forth the worlds (ŚB 11.1.6.1; AB 5.32); the seers' austerity during which Brahman came upon them (Nirukta 2.11).
Austerity as the root of all happiness; for each class its own work is its tapas — knowledge for the brāhmaṇa (MDh 11.234–235); breath-control is the highest tapas (MDh 6.70; VDh 10.5).
Faith as the sacrificer's wife, paired with truth (AB 7.10); the Agnihotra of 'truth offered in faith' (ŚB 11.3.1.4).
The trust by which one may receive good knowledge even from a lower person (MDh 2.238).

notes: Not to be confused with śrāddha, the ancestral rite (trm:sraddha-ancestral-rite).

definitions.definition: Truth as the nature of the gods, untruth of men; the vow 'I pass from untruth to truth' (ŚB 1.1.1.4–5); truth as the sacrificer (AB 7.10).
One of the common duties; speak truth that is pleasant (MDh 4.138; 10.63).
The order of which food, in the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, calls itself the firstborn (TB 2.8.8.1).

notes: U02 adds only a Brāhmaṇa usage; the Saṃhitā concept belongs to U01.

definitions.definition: The observance taken by the sacrificer on entering a rite (ŚB 1.1.1).
The vows of the Vedic student and the observances (fasts and rules) prescribed in the smṛtis and digests.
A formal verbal contest on the hidden meaning of the rite and the cosmos, as between Yājñavalkya and Śākalya (ŚB 11.6.3) or Uddālaka and Svaidāyana (ŚB 11.4.1).
In the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka, a name of the wind-girdled seers who practised austerity and celibacy (TA 2.7.1).

cross_language.note: In Pali and Jain usage the non-Vedic ascetics

definitions.definition: A member of groups living outside the Vedic sacrificial order, who may be admitted by the Vrātya rites (PB 17.1–4).
A twice-born whose initiation has lapsed ('fallen from the Sāvitrī', MDh 2.39).
The explanatory portion of a Brāhmaṇa (blame, praise, the deeds of others, ancient precedent) as distinct from injunction (ĀpŚS 24.1.33).
The Saṃhitā portion of the Veda — verses, formulas and chants — which, with the Brāhmaṇa, makes up the Veda (ĀpŚS 24.1.31); to be recited with exact accent (PŚ 52) and understood (Nirukta 1.15–18).
The prose portion of the Veda that enjoins rites and explains them; 'Veda is the name for mantra and brāhmaṇa' (ĀpŚS 24.1.31–32).

notes: The social class 'brāhmaṇa' is under trm:varna.

definitions.definition: A 'forest book' of a Vedic school, containing the dangerous or secret rites and meditations (Mahāvrata, Pravargya, saṃhitā-upaniṣads) studied away from the village, and often an Upaniṣad.
Each of the six auxiliary sciences — śikṣā, kalpa, vyākaraṇa, nirukta, chandas, jyotiṣa — pictured as the Veda's nose, hands, mouth, ear, feet and eye (PŚ 41–42).
The science of correct pronunciation of the Veda — phoneme, accent, quantity, force, evenness and connection (TU 1.2).
The science of ritual procedure, set out in the Śrauta-, Gṛhya-, Dharma- and Śulba-sūtras of each Vedic school.

notes: Id disambiguated from kalpa as a world-eon.

definitions.definition: Grammar, 'the mouth of the Veda' and chief of its limbs (PŚ 41–42; Mahābhāṣya), studied to protect and understand the Veda.
The science of explaining Vedic words, chiefly by deriving them from verbal roots — the completion of grammar (Nirukta 1.15).
The explanation of a word by relating it to a root and a meaning; one should always attend to the meaning and never fail to give one (Nirukta 2.1).

Metre, the 'feet' of the Veda (PŚ 41); so called because the gods covered (chad) themselves with the metres against death (ChU 1.4.2). In Pāṇini, also the Vedic language as opposed to ordinary speech.
In its Vedāṅga form, time-reckoning by sun, moon and lunar mansions to fix the times of sacrifice; 'at the head of the Vedāṅgas' (Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa Ṛk 3, 35).
A phonetic treatise of a particular Vedic school (śākhā), governing the relation of the word-by-word and continuous texts, sandhi and accent.
The traditional list of Vedic synonyms, obscure words and deity names on which the Nirukta comments.
The Vedic pitch accents — udātta (high), anudātta (low), svarita (combined) (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.29–31); also 'vowel'. Error in accent turns a mantra against the sacrificer (PŚ 52).

notes: The musical sense belongs to lin:sangita (U31).

definitions.definition: Vowel quantity: short, long and prolated (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.2.27); one of the six topics of phonetics (TU 1.2).
A phoneme — sixty-three or sixty-four, declared by Svayambhū (PŚ 3); the first topic of phonetics (TU 1.2).
Each of the four social classes — brāhmaṇa, kṣatriya, vaiśya, śūdra — with their duties (MDh 1.31, 1.88–91; 10.4); stated by the tradition as created from the Person's mouth, arms, thighs and feet.
In the Brāhmaṇas the classes are correlated with metres, gods, chants and animals (TS 7.1.1.4–6) and with the three Vedas (TB 3.12.9.2).

notes: Homonym: phoneme (Vedāṅga) and social class (Dharmaśāstra) kept as separate definitions.

definitions.definition: A syllable or phoneme (akṣarasamāmnāya, the list of phonemes, PŚ 57).
The imperishable syllable Oṃ, which is Brahman and Prajāpati, while all rites pass away (MDh 2.84).
A word, defined as what ends in a nominal or verbal ending (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.4.14); also a quarter of a verse.
A verbal root, listed in the Dhātupāṭha (Aṣṭādhyāyī 1.3.1: 'bhū and the rest are roots').

notes: Other senses (bodily tissue, element) belong to other units.

definitions.definition: A participant in an action as analysed by Pāṇini — agent, object, instrument, recipient, source, locus; 'the independent one is the agent' (1.4.54).
The verb, whose chief meaning is becoming (bhāva) as a sequence (Nirukta 1.1).
The noun, whose chief meaning is being (sattva) (Nirukta 1.1); all nouns derive from verbs according to Śākaṭāyana (1.12).
An abbreviation formed from the Māheśvara sūtras by a first sound and a final marker, naming a class of sounds (e.g. aC = the vowels).

The recitation of the Veda with all sandhi applied, as distinct from the word-by-word (padapāṭha) and step (kramapāṭha) recitations; its secret meaning is taught in the saṃhitā-upaniṣads (AA 3.1.1; TU 1.3).
The analysed text in which each word is recited separately without sandhi (for the Ṛgveda, Śākalya's).
Recitation in overlapping pairs of words (ab, bc, cd…), the first of the modified recitations that guard the text.
The eight elaborated recitations (jaṭā, mālā, śikhā, rekhā, dhvaja, daṇḍa, ratha, ghana) built from the step recitation.
A group of three syllables classified by its pattern of heavy and light, used to define metres (Piṅgala, ch. 1).
A Vedic metre of 24 syllables in its standard form (Piṅgala; Ṛgveda Prātiśākhya); in the Brāhmaṇas correlated with deities and classes (TS 7.1.1.4–6).
A Vedic metre of 32 syllables in its standard form (Piṅgala; Ṛgveda Prātiśākhya); in the Brāhmaṇas correlated with deities and classes (TS 7.1.1.4–6).
A Vedic metre of 44 syllables in its standard form (Piṅgala; Ṛgveda Prātiśākhya); in the Brāhmaṇas correlated with deities and classes (TS 7.1.1.4–6).
A Vedic metre of 48 syllables in its standard form (Piṅgala; Ṛgveda Prātiśākhya); in the Brāhmaṇas correlated with deities and classes (TS 7.1.1.4–6).
One of the twenty-seven (or twenty-eight) star-groups through which the moon passes, used to fix the times of rites (Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa; ŚB 2.1.2.3 on the Kṛttikās).
The five-year cycle of the Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa, presided over by Prajāpati (Ṛk 1).

The four world-ages Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara and Kali, of 4,000, 3,000, 2,000 and 1,000 divine years with twilights, in which dharma declines foot by foot (MDh 1.68–86); named already as states of a man in AB 7.15.
The period of one Manu, seventy-one ages of the gods (MDh 1.79).
The word, defined in the Mahābhāṣya as that by which, when uttered, the understanding of the thing arises.

notes: Philosophical senses (śabda-brahman, testimony) belong to U31/U11/U12.

definitions.definition: The syllable made by Prajāpati from the sounds a, u, m drawn out of the three utterances (AB 5.32); expounded at length in the Gopatha Brāhmaṇa.
The imperishable syllable, Brahman and Prajāpati, recited with the utterances and the Sāvitrī (MDh 2.76–84; VDh 10.5).
The three utterances bhūḥ, bhuvaḥ, svaḥ, spoken by Prajāpati to create earth, atmosphere and sky (ŚB 11.1.6.3), drawn from the three Vedas (AB 5.32).
The utterances recited before the Sāvitrī and in breath-control (MDh 2.76–81; YS 1.23).
The Gāyatrī verse to Savitṛ (RV 3.62.10) taught at initiation, the 'mother' of the twice-born's Vedic birth (MDh 2.170), recited at the twilights.
Repetition of a mantra; audible, whispered and mental japa are ten, a hundred and a thousand times better than ritual sacrifice (MDh 2.85–87).
The twilight rite in which water consecrated with the Gāyatrī is thrown up against the Mandeha demons and the sun is meditated on as Brahman (TA 2.2).
The obligatory morning and evening worship with bathing, sprinkling, breath-control and Gāyatrī recitation (YS 1.22–25).

Breath-control performed with Oṃ, the utterances and the Gāyatrī with its 'head' — the highest austerity, burning away the faults of the senses as smelting burns the dross of ores (MDh 6.70–72; YS 1.23; VDh 10.5).
Fixation of the mind, which burns away sin (MDh 6.72).
Withdrawal of the senses, which burns away attachments (MDh 6.72).
Meditation, which burns away the 'ungodly qualities' and lets one see the course of the inner self (MDh 6.72–73).

The discipline by which the self is seen (YS 1.8) and by which the faults that burn beings are removed (ĀpDh 1.8.23); the renouncer's practice of breath-control, fixation, withdrawal and meditation (MDh 6.70–74).
Musical sound; one who knows the vīṇā, the microtones and rhythm reaches liberation without effort (YS 3.115).

The whole of right conduct — ritual, moral, social and legal — rooted in the Veda, smṛti, the practice of the good and self-approval (MDh 2.6); it protects when protected and alone follows one after death (MDh 8.15–17; 4.238–242); its tenfold mark is steadfastness, patience, self-control, not stealing, purity, sense-restraint, wisdom, learning, truth and absence of anger (MDh 6.92).
The merit that correct usage of words brings, for which grammar restricts usage (first vārttika).
The Veda (MDh 2.10), the supreme authority for those seeking to know dharma (MDh 2.13).
The dharmaśāstra (MDh 2.10); the recollection of those who know the Veda, a source of dharma second to it.
The practice of the good (sadācāra) as a source of dharma (MDh 2.6); without it the Vedas do not purify (VDh 6.3).
The learned and virtuous whose practice is authoritative where the Veda is silent: free of envy, pride and greed, content with a pot of grain (BDh 1.1.1.5); 'free from desire' (VDh 1.6).
The council of learned brāhmaṇas that decides dharma where texts are silent — ten, three, or even one who knows the Veda or the self (MDh 12.108–113; YS 1.9).
One who reviles the Veda and relies on reasoning against it, to be expelled by the good (MDh 2.11).
Litigation and the law of the eighteen titles, which arose when dharma declined among humans (Nāradasmṛti Mātṛkā 1.1–2).
Punishment, which rules and protects all creatures and is itself dharma (MDh 7.18).
The duty proper to one's class and stage; better done imperfectly than another's done well (MDh 10.97); it leads to heaven and endlessness (Arthaśāstra 1.3.14).
The relaxed rules of livelihood and conduct permitted in emergencies (MDh 10.81ff.).

Practices once permitted by the smṛtis but declared forbidden in the Kali age by later authorities (e.g. levirate, the great departure, cow-sacrifice), justified by the principle that dharma differs by age.

literal: to be avoided in the Kali age

definitions.definition: A member of the first three classes, born a second time by initiation (MDh 2.169–171; 10.4).
Birth-group; the mixed classes arising from unions across the varṇas (anuloma, pratiloma) described in MDh 10.
Non-injury, first of the common duties of all classes (MDh 10.63; YS 1.122; Arthaśāstra 1.3.13); the Veda-prescribed injury is declared to be non-injury (MDh 5.44).
Injury to living beings; meat cannot be had without it (MDh 5.48).
One of the common duties of all (MDh 10.63).
Purity of body, mind and dealings; purity in wealth is the highest; the body is purified by water, the mind by truth (MDh 5.105–109).
The eight virtues — compassion, patience, freedom from envy, purity, calm, auspiciousness, generosity, freedom from greed — without which the forty sacraments do not lead to Brahman (GDh 8.22–25).
The safety the renouncer gives to all beings on going forth (MDh 6.39–40).
The intention in which desire is rooted and from which sacrifices and vows arise (MDh 2.3); desire born of right intention is a root of dharma (YS 1.7).
The eleven faculties — five of knowledge, five of action and mind — to be restrained like horses (MDh 2.88–92).
The self that makes the embodied self act, distinguished from the elemental self (bhūtātman) that acts (MDh 12.12).
The inner self born with the body that experiences pleasure and pain (MDh 12.13).
The self as its own witness and refuge (MDh 8.84).
One who has laid down the rods of speech, mind and body (MDh 12.10); outwardly, a renouncer carrying three staves.
Ritual action, whose fruit is secured by correct performance and knowledge.
Action of mind, speech and body, bearing good or bad fruit in high, middle or low births (MDh 12.3–9); its residue shapes the next birth (ĀpDh 2.1.2.3).
Vedic action done with desire, bringing prosperity and equality with the gods (MDh 12.88–90); the natural activity of beings (MDh 5.56).
Desireless action preceded by knowledge, leading beyond the elements to the supreme good (MDh 12.89–90); abstention, which bears great fruit (MDh 5.56).
The highest good, secured by Vedic recitation, austerity, knowledge, sense-restraint, non-injury and service of the teacher, above all by self-knowledge (MDh 12.83–85).
The three qualities of the self — sattva, rajas, tamas — determining destinies (MDh 12.24–51).
The guṇa characterized as knowledge; those in it go to the gods' state (MDh 12.26, 12.40).
The guṇa characterized as attraction and aversion; those in it go to the human state (MDh 12.26, 12.40).
The guṇa characterized as ignorance; those in it go to the animal state (MDh 12.26, 12.40).
The aims of human life — dharma, artha, kāma, and (as the fourth) mokṣa; Manu's settled view is that the good is the triad (MDh 2.224).
Of the three, artha is foremost since the others are rooted in it (Arthaśāstra 1.7.6–7).
The three are to be pursued in their proper ages without harming each other; each earlier is weightier (Kāmasūtra 1.2.1–14).
Dharma, artha and kāma taken together (MDh 2.224); later texts add mokṣa to make the caturvarga.
Wealth and power, the livelihood of the world, the aim served by the Arthaśāstra.

notes: Its sense 'meaning' (of a word) is used in the Vedāṅgas (Nirukta 2.1: 'attend always to the meaning').

definitions.definition: Desire: not praiseworthy in itself, yet no action is without it (MDh 2.2–4); never quenched by enjoyment (MDh 2.94).
The aim of love and pleasure, proper to youth, to be pursued without harming dharma and artha (Kāmasūtra 1.2).
Liberation, on which one sets the mind after paying the three debts (MDh 6.35–37), reached by renunciation, yoga and self-knowledge (MDh 6.74, 12.85).
Pursued with dharma in old age (Kāmasūtra 1.2.4).

One of the four orders: student, householder, forest-hermit, renouncer (MDh 6.87); whether they are chosen freely, followed in sequence, or whether only the householder's is Vedic is disputed (GDh 3.1–3.36; BDh 2.6.11.27; VDh 7.3; ĀpDh 2.9.21.1).

literal: stage of exertion; order of life

definitions.definition: Vedic studentship, by which the debt to the seers is paid (TS 6.3.10.5); the student is withheld from Death if he brings fuel and begs daily (ŚB 11.3.3).
The student's stage in the teacher's house, with chastity, begging and service; temporary or lifelong (naiṣṭhika).

cross_language.note: In Pali the holy life in general

definitions.definition: The householder, 'eldest' of the orders, supporting the others as air supports beings (MDh 3.77–78; 6.89–90).
The forest-hermit, entered when one sees wrinkles, grey hair and grandchildren (MDh 6.2).
Renunciation of rites and possessions after depositing the fires in oneself (MDh 6.38); the renouncer should never renounce the Veda (VDh 10.4).
The debts with which one is born — to the seers, gods and ancestors (TS 6.3.10.5), and to men (ŚB 1.7.2.1).
The three debts to be paid before seeking liberation (MDh 6.35–37).
The five great sacrifices to beings, men, ancestors, gods and Brahman (ŚB 11.5.6.1; TA 2.10).
The householder's daily five sacrifices, expiating the 'five slaughter-places' (MDh 3.68–70).
Daily Vedic self-study, the sacrifice to Brahman, praised as bringing concentration and joy (ŚB 11.5.6.3; 11.5.7.1).
Food set out daily for beings (bhūtayajña) (ŚB 11.5.6.2); offerings 'not into fire' (ĀśGS 1.1.2).
The guest, whose honouring is the sacrifice to men (MDh 3.70).
The water-offering to the ancestors (and gods and seers), the daily sacrifice to the ancestors (MDh 3.70).
A consecratory rite of passage purifying the body of the twice-born from conception to death (MDh 2.26–28); Gautama counts forty (GDh 8.14–21), later lists sixteen.

notes: Homonym: latent impression (Yoga, Buddhism) is defined by other units.

definitions.definition: Initiation in which the boy gives himself to studentship and the teacher, 'becoming pregnant', brings him to birth with the Sāvitrī (ŚB 11.5.4).
The sacrament of initiation at 8, 11 or 12 years for the three classes — the second birth (MDh 2.36, 2.169; ĀpDh 1.1.1.9).
The teacher who initiates and teaches the Veda with its ritual and secret parts, 'from whom one gathers the dharmas' (ĀpDh 1.1.1.14); ten times more venerable than a sub-teacher (MDh 2.145).
One who teaches a part of the Veda or its limbs for a living (MDh 2.141).
One learned in the Veda, who is 'great among us' regardless of age or wealth (MDh 2.154).
One who 'saw' the hymns; Brahman the self-existent came upon them in their austerity (Nirukta 2.11); they had direct vision of dharma (Nirukta 1.20).
The seers are the breaths (ŚB 6.1.1.1; AA 2.2.1).
Marriage, of eight forms (MDh 3.21), performed with the customs of region and village (ĀśGS 1.7.1).
The appointment of a widow or wife to bear a son by a brother-in-law or sapiṇḍa; permitted and then condemned in Manu (9.59–68).
The funeral rite — cremation (or burial of infants), bone-collection, water-offerings and the rites of the first year.
The offering of food and piṇḍas to the ancestors with feeding of brāhmaṇas, monthly on the new moon and on other occasions (MDh 3.122–286).
The rice-ball offered to the father, grandfather and great-grandfather in the ancestral rites.
The ancestors, who receive food monthly, svadhā as drink, the moon as their light (ŚB 2.4.2.2).
The primeval deities of several classes (Somasads, Agniṣvāttas, Barhiṣads…) (MDh 3.192–199).
The newly dead, not yet united with the ancestors, sustained by the first-year offerings until the sapiṇḍīkaraṇa.
The rite (on the twelfth day or after a year) that unites the deceased with his three forefathers, turning the preta into a pitṛ.
A kinsman within seven generations (MDh 5.60); defined by shared bodily particles in the Mitākṣarā and by shared piṇḍa-offerings in the Dāyabhāga.
The ritual impurity of relatives after a birth or death, lasting ten days for sapiṇḍas (MDh 5.59) or by class (5.83).
The exclamation with which offerings go to the ancestors, their 'drink' (ŚB 2.4.2.2; 11.5.6.2).

literal: one's own power; the ancestors' call

definitions.definition: Rites and penances removing the stain of sin — needed by one who omits the enjoined, does the forbidden or is attached to objects (MDh 11.44); by confession, remorse, austerity, recitation and gifts (MDh 11.227).
The five great sins: killing a brāhmaṇa, drinking liquor, theft (of gold), violating the teacher's bed, and associating with such sinners (MDh 11.54).
A class of expiatory penances regulating food over a set number of days (MDh 11.211–215) — restricted content.
The penance in which food follows the waning and waxing moon (MDh 11.216) — restricted content.
The hour before dawn for waking and reflecting on dharma, artha and the meaning of the Veda (MDh 4.92).
Days and circumstances (storms, deaths, festivals, the moon's days) on which Vedic recitation is suspended (MDh 4.101–127).
